The queried edge 3, between B and C, is in the accent color, as are the ids 2 and 3 of its endpoints. The card returns the Edge object Edge(id=3, 2 -> 3)." width="100%"} Retrieves the `Edge` object for the specified edge ID. The `Edge` object has five properties: - `id`: the integer edge ID - `source` and `target`: the integer node IDs of the endpoints (not their labels) - `weight`: the edge weight as a float, or `None` if no `weight=` was given when the edge was added - `attributes`: a dict of the edge's other attributes (such as `rel` or `type`), or `None` if it has none Use it to inspect everything stored on one edge, e.g. after finding its ID with `find_edge_ids()` or `get_edge_ids()`. If you only need the endpoints, `get_node_ids_by_edge_id()` returns them directly; to see all edges at once, use `get_edge_df()`. In an undirected graph, `source` and `target` simply record the order in which the endpoints were given to `add_edge()`. As with `get_node()`, the `attributes` dict is a copy, so changing it doesn't change the graph; use `set_edge_attrs()` for that. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [edge_id]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The integer ID of the edge to retrieve. Edge IDs are assigned automatically, starting at `1`, in the order edges are added. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Edge]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The `Edge` object. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [EdgeNotFoundError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If no edge has this ID (a subclass of both `ValueError` and `KeyError`). ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} `get_edge()` looks up an edge by its ID and returns the underlying `Edge` object, whose `source`/`target` are resolved node IDs rather than the original labels: ::: {#6be42d5d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_edge("A", "B", weight=1.5, type="friend") ) edge_ids = graph.get_edge_ids() edge = graph.get_edge(edge_ids[0]) edge.source, edge.target ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (1, 2) ``` ::: ::: `weight` and `attributes` are also available directly on the edge. The weight is kept separately, so `attributes` holds only the remaining keyword arguments: ::: {#6e08e820 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} edge.weight, edge.attributes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1.5, {'type': 'friend'}) ``` ::: ::: A common pattern is to find an edge's ID from its endpoints with `find_edge_ids()` and then fetch the full edge. Here the edge was added as `"C"` to `"B"`, which is the orientation the `Edge` object reports (`3 -> 2`): ::: {#3e880947 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "B", {"rel": "road"})]) ) edge_id = graph.find_edge_ids("B", "C")[0] graph.get_edge(edge_id) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` Edge(id=2, 3 -> 2) ``` ::: ::: An edge ID that doesn't exist raises; `has_edge_id()` checks first: ::: {#55c9364d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.has_edge_id(99) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` False ``` ::: :::
